meta.title: Who really said "A person who never made a mistake never tried anything new"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Einstein — no source exists, and the earliest Einstein credit Quote Investigator found is a Syracuse newspaper in 1995, forty years after his death. The saying is a Victorian commonplace: Samuel Smiles wrote a version in 1859, and Theodore Roosevelt was using another by 1900.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A person who never made a mistake never tried anything new'?
meta.ogDescription: No Einstein source has ever been produced. The idea is Victorian self-help — Samuel Smiles, 1859 — and the Einstein credit only shows up in 1995.

answer.label: Nobody famous — a Victorian commonplace
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · the family of sayings runs back to 1832
answer.sourceLine: There is no Einstein source — not a letter, a lecture, an interview or a reported remark. The saying belongs to a Victorian self-help family that predates him: Samuel Smiles wrote ‘he who never made a mistake, never made a discovery’ in 1859, an unattributed version using the word ‘tried’ was circulating by 1901, and Theodore Roosevelt was quoted using a variant in 1900. The earliest Einstein credit Quote Investigator has found is a 1995 newspaper — forty years after he died.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: He who never made a mistake, never made a discovery.
trail: The oldest relative located is from The New Sporting Magazine in 1832, unattributed: ‘He who never makes an effort, never risks a failure.’ The shape of the thought is already there, twenty-seven years before Smiles and forty-seven before Einstein was born the trace ↗.

Samuel Smiles gave it its most quotable Victorian form in Self-Help (1859). Theodore Roosevelt’s biographer Jacob Riis recorded him using another variant in 1900 — ‘the only man who never makes a mistake is the man who never does anything’ — which was already in circulation before Roosevelt picked it up.

A closer-worded named instance turns up in 1889: the London magazine Punch reported an American minister, a Mr. Phelps, saying ‘a man who never makes a mistake will never make anything’ at a farewell banquet — nearer the modern line than Smiles, and with a name attached, though not Einstein’s the trace ↗.

The Einstein connection is the newest part of the story, not the oldest. The first linkage located is the Syracuse Herald-Journal in 1995. Quote Investigator found no earlier Einstein source, and Wikiquote’s editors record no original source for it either — the earliest trace they log is an internet post from 1996.
source.excerptNote: Smiles’s version, and the earliest named ancestor this saying has — though a closer-worded line was reported of an American minister, a Mr. Phelps, in Punch, 1889. Note the difference in ambition: Smiles is talking about discovery — the scientist’s bargain, where errors are the cost of finding anything at all. The modern rewrite widens it to ‘anything new,’ which is friendlier and vaguer.

source.rightsNote: We are omitting a rights status here, because there is no single text to assign one to. The Victorian ancestors — the 1832 magazine, Smiles in 1859, the 1900 and 1901 versions — are long out of copyright and free to quote. The modern wording on this page is an anonymous drift with no identifiable author or first publication, so no term can be calculated for it. Einstein’s own writings are a separate question that does not arise, because none of this is his. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) is the default author for any encouraging remark about intelligence, failure or curiosity, which is why Princeton University Press’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein devotes entire sections to things he probably or definitely did not say. The pull here is specific: a saying that forgives mistakes lands harder from the cleverest man of the century, and the myth that he failed school maths — itself false — makes the fit feel natural. Neither the fit nor the myth is evidence.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Nothing exotic went wrong here. A common Victorian sentiment lost its authors, floated free for most of a century, and got adopted in the 1990s by the most quotable scientist available.

items.why: No letter, lecture, interview or reported remark. The earliest Einstein linkage Quote Investigator has found is a 1995 newspaper — four decades after his death — and Wikiquote’s editors log no original source for it either the trace ↗.

‘He who never made a mistake, never made a discovery’ (1859) is genuinely his and genuinely earlier. It is not this sentence — ‘discovery’ is narrower than ‘anything new’ — so he is the earliest named ancestor rather than the source. A closer-worded line — ‘a man who never makes a mistake will never make anything’ — was reported of an American minister, a Mr. Phelps, at a banquet in Punch, February 1889.

items.who: Used a variant, did not coin it
items.why: Riis recorded him saying ‘the only man who never makes a mistake is the man who never does anything’ in 1900. It was already circulating; Roosevelt spread it rather than started it.

items.scope: Benjamin Franklin, Josh Billings, Joseph Conrad
items.why: Names attach themselves to sayings of this shape the way iron filings attach to a magnet. Conrad and Billings used related lines of their own; Franklin has no documented connection at all.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous saying with Victorian ancestry — Smiles in 1859, an unattributed ‘tried’ version by 1901. The Einstein credit appears in 1995 and has no source behind it the trace ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It reframes failure as evidence rather than verdict — if you have never got anything wrong, the problem is not your record but your ambition. That is a genuinely useful reframe, and it is why the saying keeps being reinvented in every generation’s self-help vocabulary.

The false credit does real work too. Attached to Einstein, it stops being advice and starts being testimony: the man who was right about the universe telling you that being wrong is the price of admission. That is a much stronger claim, and it is the one thing about the quote that is not true.
detailsBody: 1832: The New Sporting Magazine, unattributed — ‘He who never makes an effort, never risks a failure.’
1859: Samuel Smiles, Self-Help — ‘he who never made a mistake, never made a discovery.’
1889: Punch reports a Mr. Phelps at a banquet — ‘a man who never makes a mistake will never make anything’ — the closest named wording.
1900: Theodore Roosevelt, recorded by Jacob Riis, using a variant already in circulation.
1901: a version using the word ‘tried’ appears, still with no author attached.
1995: the first located Einstein credit, in the Syracuse Herald-Journal.
context.pull: The saying is nearly two centuries old. The Einstein credit is thirty.
